title: Screenshot evidence - why courts reject most of it
p1:
A screenshot can look like undeniable proof. But in court, it may be worth far less than you think.

That WhatsApp message, Instagram conversation, payment confirmation or threatening text you saved? Simply showing it to a judge does not automatically make it admissible evidence.
p2:
Here is something many people miss: A screenshot can be genuine and still be rejected as evidence.

Why? Because the court may need to know whether it was altered, where it came from, who actually sent the message and whether the original electronic record can be verified.

Under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, electronic records must satisfy specific conditions for admissibility. The prescribed certificate is generally required when a computer output is submitted as evidence.
p3:
Think about it this way: A screenshot shows what appeared on your screen. It does not necessarily establish who created it or whether the conversation is complete.

A practical tip: Preserve the original device, retain the complete conversation, avoid editing or cropping screenshots, and obtain the required certificate when applicable.

One small mistake in preserving digital evidence can weaken an otherwise strong case.
conclusion: If someone sends you an abusive or threatening WhatsApp message, would you know how to preserve it so that it can actually be used in court?
